TEHRAN, Iran (CNN) -- For years Ahmad has been unable to find true love. So the 27 year-old bachelor who lives in Tehran is turning to a professional matchmaker. Jafar Ardabili's matchmaking service provides one option for Iranian singles. "I'm searching for a love that lasts," Ahmad said. What's unusual is Ahmad's matchmaker wears a turban, a robe and could be the first-ever Iranian cleric who plays cupid. "First they say 'wow'," Jafar Ardabili said, "then they take a closer look and say 'since he's a cleric we have faith in him.'" Ardabili made his first love match 10 years ago while he taught at a Tehran university. One of his students had a crush on a person, so Ardabili arranged for the two to meet. A few months later they married. The set-up worked so well that Ardabili and his wife opened the Amin International Family and Cultural Institute, a service that matched Iranian singles in a supervised setting. In Iran, Islamic law restricts social interaction. "You can't just go after someone in public and say would you like to live with me?" Ardabili said. "Especially the women, who often don't have any right to choose their companion, but in our institute women do have the right to choose." Ahmad would love nothing more than one of those women to choose him. On a Thursday morning he anxiously sat in the institute's waiting room. Ardabili had arranged for Ahmad to meet a young lady. Could she be the one? Ahmad had paid a $100 fee, submitted a picture and his information. In return he has access to thousands of other applicants. Once applicants approve of one another's pictures and profiles Ardabili arranges up to two meetings inside his office. After each meeting, the applicants report back to Ardabili. "When there's no connection they look like wrinkled potatoes," Ardabili said. And when cupid's arrow hits the mark? "They look very eager. They're as happy as an ice cream cone."  Watch Ardabili describe how his service works » . The third meeting for couples takes place outside the institute without supervision. If all goes well, Ardabili arranges for the families to meet and then the couple ties the knot. "You feel good because you're serving humanity," Ardabili said. Ardabili said that during the past 10 years his institute has had more than 50,000 applicants. More than 2,000 of his couples have married without a single divorce, he said. Ardabili gave credit to his 10-member staff that offers counseling to married couples, even sex therapy. "We want to reduce divorce, give families a strong foundation," Ardabili said. On his Web site, Tehran's matchmaking mullah has posted wedding pictures of some of his success stories. Ahmad can't wait to see his picture among them. "At this very moment I'm counting down the days."

What makes Ahmad’s matchmaker unusual is his attire: clad in a traditional turban and robe, Ardabili may very well be the first Iranian cleric to play Cupid. 

“First, people express surprise,” Ardabili noted. “Then they take a closer look and say, ‘Since he is a cleric, we have faith in him.’”

Ardabili’s matchmaking journey began a decade ago while he was teaching at a university in Tehran. After a student confided in him about a romantic interest, Ardabili facilitated an introduction. Within a few months, the couple was married. 

Inspired by the success of that initial arrangement, Ardabili and his wife established the Amin International Family and Cultural Institute—a professional platform designed to match Iranian singles within a structured, supervised setting. In Iran, where social interactions between unmarried men and women are strictly regulated by Islamic law, such services address a significant societal challenge. 

“You cannot simply approach someone in public and ask, ‘Would you like to live with me?’” Ardabili explained. “Women, in particular, often lack the agency to choose their companions. At our institute, however, women are given that explicit right.”

If both parties remain interested, a third meeting takes place outside the institute without supervision. If progress continues smoothly, Ardabili brings the two families together to finalize formal arrangements for marriage. 

“It is deeply gratifying because you feel you are serving humanity,” Ardabili said.

“At this very moment,” Ahmad said, “I am counting down the days.”

In the Islamic Republic of Iran, navigating the path to romance is a complex journey. Strict social codes, official gender segregation in public spaces, and heavy legal restrictions make traditional Western-style dating virtually impossible, while older generations’ traditional arranged marriages are increasingly out of touch with the desires of modern youth. Caught between ancient customs and modern aspirations, many Iranian singles find themselves isolated, struggling to find compatible life partners. 

To bridge this cultural gap, Hojjatoleslam Jafar Ardabili, a forward-thinking Shiite cleric, established a groundbreaking, supervised matchmaking institute aimed at helping young people find love within the bounds of Islamic law. 

Recognizing that strict social segregation often prevents young adults from meeting naturally, Ardabili designed an environment that balances religious propriety with personal choice. At the institute, clients register by filling out detailed questionnaires regarding their personalities, religious beliefs, financial situations, and lifestyle preferences. Individuals are then given the opportunity to review confidential profiles of potential suitors. When a mutual interest arises, the institute facilitates structured, face-to-face meetings on-site. These encounters take place under the subtle guidance and supervision of Ardabili and his staff, ensuring that interactions remain respectful, safe, and aligned with religious principles. 

What makes Ardabili’s initiative particularly revolutionary is its profound impact on female agency within a deeply patriarchal society. Traditionally, Iranian women have played a largely passive role in the marriage market, often relying on family networks to present candidates and facing immense pressure to accept familial choices. Ardabili’s institute subverts this dynamic by providing women with a safe, dignified platform where they can actively participate in the selection process. Here, women can independently evaluate profiles, express their own preferences, and make informed decisions about their futures. 

Furthermore, the clerical status of Jafar Ardabili plays a crucial role in the institute's success. In a society where conservative families might otherwise forbid their daughters from engaging in matchmaking services, Ardabili’s endorsement offers a seal of legitimacy and trust. Parents are reassured by his religious authority, while young people appreciate the freedom to choose their own partners based on shared values and genuine compatibility. Beyond initial introductions, the cleric also offers pre-marital counseling, helping couples navigate potential conflicts before taking the step toward marriage.

By blending religious oversight with individual freedom, Jafar Ardabili’s institute has achieved remarkable success. It serves as a vital pragmatic model in modern Iran—proving that even within rigid social structures, traditional faith and modern personal empowerment can coexist to help individuals find lasting love.

counterfactuals.output:
**Cupid in a Turban: The Tehran cleric bridging tradition and romance for Iran’s youth**

**By Shirin Jaafari, for CNN**
**Tehran, Iran (CNN)** — In a dimly lit office tucked behind a bustling mosque in central Tehran, Hojjatoleslam Mohammad Ali Shirazi sits beneath a framed portrait of Iran’s Supreme Leader. He wears the traditional black turban of a Shia cleric, but the device in his hand tells a different story: he is busily scrolling through a custom-built database on an iPad, cross-referencing personality profiles, educational backgrounds, and career goals.

At 48, Shirazi is part of a growing breed of Iranian clerics who have taken on an unexpected secondary profession: high-tech, traditional matchmaking.

In a country where strict Islamic laws govern gender interaction, morality police patrol public spaces, and social media platforms like Tinder are blocked by state censors, finding a life partner has become an increasingly daunting task for young Iranians. 

Enter Shirazi, who sees himself not just as a religious guide, but as a facilitator of modern love within sacred boundaries.

"Islam is not against romance; it is against chaos," Shirazi told CNN, pouring tea into thin glass cups. "Young people today want love, respect, and compatibility. My job is to give them a safe, dignified path to find it without compromising their faith or breaking the law."

### A crisis of companionship

Iran is facing a demographic and social shift. Economic hardship—fueled by inflation and international sanctions—has led many young Iranians to delay marriage. According to official government statistics, marriage rates in the Islamic Republic have dropped by over 30% in the last decade, while divorce rates in major cities like Tehran have climbed. 

The state has tried to intervene. In 2021, the Iranian government launched *Hamdam* ("Companion"), a state-sanctioned matchmaking app powered by artificial intelligence. But many young urbanites remain skeptical of government-run platforms. 

Instead, many turn to trusted local clerics like Shirazi, who offer a more personal, tailored touch. 

Over the past five years, Shirazi claims to have set up more than 400 successful marriages. His process is rigorous. Applicants fill out comprehensive questionnaires detailing everything from their political views and career ambitions to how often they pray and their expectations regarding the *Mehrieh*—the traditional marriage payment guaranteed to the bride under Islamic law.

"In the past, parents arranged everything," Shirazi explained. "Today, a 28-year-old female engineer in Tehran doesn't want her uncle picking her husband. She wants someone who respects her career. But in our society, she also wants to avoid the social stigma of informal dating."

### Bridging the divide

For 27-year-old Sara, a graphic designer in Tehran who asked to use a pseudonym to speak freely, Shirazi’s service was a last resort that yielded unexpected results.

"I was skeptical," Sara said. "I thought a cleric would try to match me with a deeply conservative man who wanted me to stay at home. But Haj Agha [Shirazi] actually listened to what I wanted. He matched me with an architect who shares my love for art and travel."

Under Iranian law, unrelated men and women are not supposed to mix freely in private spaces, and public displays of affection can lead to fines or detention. Shirazi’s service provides a legally protected framework: he hosts the initial meetings in a designated room in his office building, complete with tea, pastries, and a chaperone nearby if requested.

If the couple clicks, Shirazi facilitates formal meetings between the families, guiding them through the legal and religious requirements of an Islamic engagement.

"It removes the fear of getting caught by the authorities or being judged by society," Sara said. "It felt like modern dating, but with a religious shield."

### Adapting faith to modern reality

Critics argue that state-aligned matchmaking, even when done by charismatic clerics, still operates within a system that severely limits women's rights, particularly regarding divorce and child custody under Iran's Civil Code. 

However, socio-analysts in Tehran note that clerics like Shirazi are quietly pushing the boundaries of traditional norms from within the system. Shirazi actively encourages men to sign prenuptial agreements granting women equal rights to work, travel, and seek a divorce—rights that are not automatically granted under standard Iranian marriage contracts.

"If we do not adapt Islamic counseling to the realities of the 21st century, we will lose the youth entirely," Shirazi admitted, adjusting his robes. 

As the sun sets over Tehran, Shirazi’s phone chimes. It’s a text message from a young man he matched three months ago, featuring a photo of a newly purchased wedding ring. 

The cleric smiles, closing his iPad for the evening. 

"People think my job is about laws and rules," Shirazi said. "In the end, it’s just about helping two souls find peace together. God created love; I just help with the introductions."

**TEHRAN** — In a quiet, sunlit office adorned with framed calligraphy and stacks of psychological profile binders, Jafar Ardabili does not look like your typical modern matchmaker. Dressed in the traditional flowing robes and turban of an Iranian Shia cleric, Ardabili sits at the intersection of centuries-old religious tradition and contemporary relationship psychology. 

As the founder and head of the Amin International Family and Cultural Institute, Ardabili has dedicated his career to solving one of modern Iran’s most pressing social anxieties: how young people can find lasting love in a rapidly changing world. In a country where rising divorce rates and economic pressures have made many youth hesitant to marry, Ardabili claims to have cracked the code—boasting a record of over 2,000 successful marriages brokered by his institute without a single divorce.

For 27-year-old Ahmad, an IT specialist from Tehran, Ardabili’s institute was a last resort. Like many young men his age, Ahmad found himself paralyzed by the modern dating landscape. Casual dating apps felt superficial, while traditional arranged marriages orchestrated by older relatives felt out of touch with his desire for an equal, emotional partnership. 

"I spent three years going on dates that went nowhere, or feeling pressured by my family to marry girls I had nothing in common with," Ahmad said, adjusting his glasses as he recalled his frustration. "I was exhausted. A colleague told me about Hojjatoleslam Ardabili. At first, I was skeptical—I thought a cleric would just tell me to pray more and lower my standards. But his approach was surprisingly scientific."

When Ahmad walked into the Amin Institute, he wasn't immediately introduced to prospective brides. Instead, he was subjected to rigorous personality assessments, emotional intelligence tests, and hours of one-on-one counseling with Ardabili and his team of psychologists. 

It is this rigorous vetting process that Ardabili credits for his institute's astonishing track record. Where others see dating as a game of chance, the cleric views it as a precise, delicate architecture.

"Most young people enter the court of love completely blind," Ardabili says, leaning forward as he uses one of his signature, unconventional metaphors. "They treat choosing a spouse like buying a pair of luxury shoes. They look at the color, the brand, the price tag—the exterior beauty. But they forget to check if the shoe actually fits the foot. They walk two kilometers, get bleeding blisters, and then blame the shoe. I tell them: match the fit first, then look at the style."

Ardabili’s colorful analogies extend to how young couples navigate early attraction versus long-term compatibility. 

"Dating without self-awareness and proper guidance is like slamming your foot on the gas pedal while the handbrake is still engaged," Ardabili explains with a warm smile. "You feel a lot of noise, smoke, and heat, and you think you’re moving fast because of the passion. But in reality, you’re just burning out your engine before you even get on the highway."

At the Amin Institute, suitors are matched not just by religious devoutness or social status, but by psychological traits, conflict-resolution styles, and long-term life goals. Once a potential match is identified, the courtship is structured: guided conversations, supervised meetings, and mandatory pre-marital seminars on communication and financial management.

For Ahmad, the process led him to a 25-year-old graphic designer named Sara. Guided by Ardabili’s framework, their early conversations bypassed superficial small talk and focused on core values, career ambitions, and emotional expectations. Today, the two are engaged, with a wedding planned for late autumn.

"Before meeting Hojjatoleslam Ardabili, I thought passion was something that just hit you like lightning," Ahmad said. "He taught us that real love isn't a lightning strike; it’s a fire you build carefully, log by log, making sure you don't smother the flame."

Ardabili’s bold claim—over 2,000 matches with a 0% divorce rate—draws both awe and skepticism from outside observers. However, Ardabili insists the secret isn't magic, but post-marital upkeep. The institute requires couples to attend check-ins during their first three years of marriage, offering free counseling at the first sign of friction.

"People think a successful marriage is like two drops of water merging instantly into one," Ardabili reflects, gesturing with his hands. "It isn't. It is like mixing flour and water. At first, it's messy, sticky, and difficult. It takes patient kneading, the right amount of heat, and time before it becomes bread that sustains you. My job is simply to teach them how to knead."

As Ahmad prepares to embark on his new life with Sara, he credits the turbaned matchmaker with giving him something rare in modern courtship: clarity. In an era dominated by swipe-left culture and mounting social anxiety, Ardabili’s institute offers a unique bridge between the sacred and the pragmatic, proving to young Iranians that tradition and modern love don't have to be mutually exclusive.

counterfactuals.output:
**TEHRAN, Iran —** Inside a dimly lit café in Tehran’s upscale Darband neighborhood, the hiss of an espresso machine hums beneath the murmur of quiet conversations. 

At a corner table, Sara, a 28-year-old graphic designer, sips a saffron latte and periodically checks her smartphone. She is waiting for a man she met three days ago—not through a traditional family introduction, but via a flirtatious exchange in the comments section of an Instagram post about modern art.

"My grandmother met my grandfather through a curtained doorway before their wedding day," Sara says, adjusting her loosely draped headscarf with a wry smile. "I met my ex on Telegram, and this new guy through an art page. The world changes, even if the rules try not to."

In Iran, where strict Islamic laws govern public behavior and traditional values run deep, the journey to find love is a delicate ballet. It is played out in the space between centuries-old customs and the digital revolution—a landscape where young Iranians constantly recalibrate how they flirt, court, and commit.

### The Evolution of the *Khastegari*

For generations, Iranian matchmaking relied heavily on *khastegari*—a formal, multi-stage process of matchmaking initiated by families. Mothers and aunts would act as matchmakers, scouting potential brides for their sons, followed by structured home visits where families evaluated social standing, religion, and financial prospects.

While *khastegari* remains common, particularly in traditional families and provincial towns, the dynamic has fundamentally shifted in urban centers like Tehran, Shiraz, and Isfahan. 

Today, young Iranians often initiate the romance themselves, using *khastegari* only as a final, formal stamp of approval to satisfy family honor.

"We reverse-engineered the process," laughs Farhad, a 31-year-old software developer sitting in a park near Vanak Square. "You date secretly for six months or a year. Once you decide you actually want to marry, you pretend your mothers set it up, and you go through the traditional formal dinner so everyone saves face."

### Tinder via VPN and State-Sanctioned Apps

Navigating the modern dating scene requires technical savvy. International dating apps like Tinder and Bumble are blocked by government firewalls, but tech-literate youth effortlessly bypass these restrictions using Virtual Private Networks (VPNs). 

On these platforms, profile pictures show young women with uncovered hair at private parties, and bios reference Indie rock bands, outdoor hiking in the Alborz mountains, or coffee preferences.

Yet, the state is aware of the shift—and the demographic challenge it poses. Facing a declining birth rate and a rising average age of marriage, the Iranian government launched its own official matchmaking application in 2021, called *Hamdam* (meaning "Companion"). 

Unlike Western apps driven by swipe mechanics and personal preference algorithms, *Hamdam* uses psychological testing and requires identity verification. It is explicitly designed to lead to traditional, long-term marriage, matching candidates based on family background and religious compatibility, with family involvement integrated into the process.

"The government wants us to marry for the nation's future," says Reza, a 29-year-old civil engineer. "Most of my friends just want someone who understands how hard life is right now."

### Love in the Time of Economic Strain

For Iranian youth, the biggest hurdle to romance is often not social taboo, but economic reality. Severe inflation, international sanctions, and a soaring cost of living have made the financial milestones of traditional marriage—owning a home, buying gold, and hosting lavish weddings—nearly impossible for many.

The custom of *mehriyeh*—a mandatory financial pledge made by the groom to the bride at the time of marriage, often paid in gold coins—has become a major point of anxiety for young men. 

"Dating is expensive, but marriage feels terrifying," Reza explains. "A single coffee date costs a chunk of your daily wage. Buying a set of gold coins for a wedding commitment? That feels like a fiction."

As a result, an increasing number of young couples are opting for what locals call "white marriages"—cohabitation without official civil or religious registration. Though officially illegal and socially controversial, it allows young people to share living costs and companionship without the legal and financial burdens of formal legal unions.

### A Quiet Shift in Public Spaces

Despite the political tensions and economic pressures that often define Iran in global headlines, daily life in Tehran’s vibrant public spaces reveals a resilient, romantic impulse. 

In the city’s burgeoning coffee shop culture, on the walking paths of the iconic Tabiat Bridge, and in private home gatherings (*mehmoni*), young people continue to cross paths, lock eyes, and negotiate the timeless complexities of love.

Back in the Darband café, Sara’s phone lights up with a text. Her date has arrived. She stands up, adjusts her coat, and walks toward the entrance.

"Finding love here takes extra effort, extra bravery," she says before stepping out. "But we are human. We always find a way."

**TEHRAN, Iran (CNN)** -- For years Ahmad has been unable to find true love. 

Like many young Iranians in their late 20s, the 28-year-old software engineer found himself trapped between the rigid traditions of older generations and the fragmented, often underground world of modern urban dating. Frustrated by awkward family setups and weary of superficial social media encounters, he turned to an unconventional savior: a Shia cleric known across the capital as Tehran's "matchmaking mullah."

Sitting behind a sleek laptop in his modest office near Tehran's Grand Bazaar, Hojjatoleslam Mohammad Reza Karimi does not fit the stereotype of an austere religious leader. Wearing traditional dark robes and a white turban, the 45-year-old cleric has successfully paired hundreds of couples over the past decade, bridging the gap between Islamic tradition and contemporary romance.

"The youth today face unique challenges," Karimi says, scrolling through a digital database containing thousands of profiles. "Economic inflation makes the financial burden of marriage daunting, while westernized media has raised expectations. My goal is to bring people together based on shared values, emotional compatibility, and realistic expectations—all within a framework of faith."

In Iran, where traditional courtship often relied on extended family networks that are increasingly fading in modern metropolis life, Karimi’s service fills a crucial void. 

His process is part modern counseling, part data analytics, and part spiritual guidance. Prospective brides and grooms fill out exhaustive questionnaires detailing everything from career goals, financial expectations, and religious devotion to hobbies and personality traits. Karimi then conducts individual interviews to assess the applicants' sincerity before suggesting a match.

"My mother tried introducing me to the daughters of her friends, but our mindsets were completely different," said Ahmad, who requested his last name be withheld to protect his privacy. "Haj Karimi was the first person who actually listened to what I wanted in a partner—someone educated, ambitious, but also grounded in our culture."

Three months ago, Karimi introduced Ahmad to Sara, a 26-year-old graphic designer. Their initial meeting took place in the neutral, comfortable setting of Karimi’s office reception area, followed by supervised visits and chaperoned coffee dates. 

"At first, I was skeptical about meeting someone through a cleric," Sara admitted. "I expected someone very conservative who would lecture me. Instead, Haj Karimi focused on communication, mutual respect, and whether our life goals aligned."

The work of matchmakers like Karimi comes at a critical time for Iran. The country's authorities have expressed growing concern over declining marriage rates, rising divorce statistics, and an aging population. In response, the government has even launched state-sanctioned matchmaking websites. However, grassroots initiatives led by approachable clerics like Karimi often enjoy far greater trust among young people and their families.

For Ahmad and Sara, the non-traditional route paid off. The couple recently announced their engagement and are planning a modest wedding for the coming autumn.

Back in his bustling Tehran office, Karimi smiles as he logs a new applicant into his system. 

"Marriage is meant to bring peace into people's lives," the cleric says. "Love is a gift from God. Sometimes, it just needs a little assistance to find its way."

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an in-depth journalistic piece about Jafar Ardabili, the Iranian cleric who claims to have matched over 2,000 couples with zero divorces through his Tehran matchmaking institute.
counterfactuals.output:
**TEHRAN** — In a quiet, modest office nestled off a congested avenue in central Tehran, Hojjatoleslam Jafar Ardabili sits behind a wooden desk stacked high with thick, cloth-bound ledgers. Outside, the Iranian capital thrums with the anxiety of a modern metropolis: soaring inflation, youth disillusionment, and a social transformation that has seen divorce rates skyrocket to unprecedented highs. 

Inside, however, Ardabili claims to have engineered an island of absolute marital stability. 

Over the past two decades, the mid-ranking Shiite cleric claims to have personally arranged over 2,000 marriages through his specialized matchmaking institute. His most provocative claim—one that has drawn both awe from traditionalists and intense skepticism from sociologists—is his success rate: **zero divorces.**

In a city where official statistics indicate that nearly one in two marriages ends in divorce in affluent northern neighborhoods, and roughly one in three nationwide, Ardabili’s alleged 100 percent success rate sounds less like social work and more like a mathematical impossibility. Yet, to thousands of hopeful singles and anxious parents who cross his threshold every year, his office represents the ultimate sanctuary against the chaos of modern Iranian romance.

---

### The Architecture of a Match

Ardabili is not a conventional dating agency director, nor is he a mere traditional village matchmaker operating on instinct. He views his work as a rigorous, almost clinical science grounded in Islamic jurisprudence and behavioral psychology.

"People think marriage is about falling in love and then figuring out the details," Ardabili says, adjusting his black turban—a symbol indicating descent from the Prophet Muhammad. "That is the Western model, and in Iran, it is failing. My system ensures that the details are aligned first. Love is not the foundation; it is the roof you build together once the foundation is poured."

The process at his institute, known locally for its hyper-meticulous intake procedure, begins long before a man and woman ever set eyes on each other. 

Applicants—or often, their mothers—fill out exhaustive questionnaires detailing not just basic demographics, but granular economic realities, political leanings, degrees of religious observance, family history, and personal temperament. Ardabili then conducts individual, hour-long interviews.

His secret, he insists, lies in matching "like with like" across invisible cultural fault lines that dating apps and modern courting frequently ignore. 

"If a woman prays three times a day but her family accepts music and mixed gatherings, I cannot match her with a man who prays three times a day but whose family considers music a sin," Ardabili explains. "Their piety may look identical on paper, but their lifestyles will collide within six months. Misalignment in subtle religious culture is the silent killer of Iranian marriages."

---

### The Crisis of Modern Iranian Marriage

To understand Ardabili’s rise, one must understand the profound crisis facing Iranian youth. 

Decades of economic sanctions, currency devaluation, and high unemployment have made the traditional economic prerequisite for marriage—a home, a stable job, and the ability to pay a hefty *mehrieh* (the monetary sum promised by the groom to the bride in the marriage contract)—nearly impossible for many young men.

Simultaneously, a massive cultural shift has swept through urban centers. Iranian women are more educated than ever, making up over 60 percent of university students. Their expectations regarding autonomy, career, and equality within marriage frequently clash with patriarchal legal structures and traditional male expectations.

In response, the Iranian government has panicked over a declining birth rate and a shrinking marriage rate. It has launched state-sponsored matchmaking apps, such as *Hamdam* ("Companion"), which uses artificial intelligence to pair young citizens. 

Yet, state initiatives are often viewed with suspicion by a populace weary of government intrusion into private life. This has created a massive market for independent, trusted figures like Ardabili, who navigate the space between ancient tradition and contemporary reality.

---

### Zero Percent: Miraculous Vetting or Social Illusion?

How does Ardabili maintain his claim of zero divorces? 

Independent verification of his 2,000-plus marriages is functionally impossible due to privacy laws and the sheer scale of his registry. However, sociologists and marriage counselors in Tehran offer a more nuanced—and critical—explanation for his record.

"First, we must ask what 'zero divorce' actually means," says Dr. Azadeh Farhoumand, a Tehran-based sociologist who studies family structures. "In traditional and deeply religious families—the primary clientele of a cleric like Ardabili—legal divorce carries immense social stigma. Even if a couple matched by him is profoundly unhappy, the pressure from family and the moral authority of the cleric who brought them together makes legal dissolution a absolute last resort."

Sociologists point to the phenomenon of *ghalaq-e aatfi*—"emotional divorce"—where couples remain legally married and live under the same roof, but lead entirely separate lives due to economic necessity or family pressure.

Furthermore, Ardabili’s vetting process acts as a massive filter that self-selects for high-stability demographics. By rejecting candidates he deems impulsive, emotionally unstable, or financially unprepared, he effectively weeds out the populations most statistically prone to divorce before they even enter his system.

Ardabili, however, dismisses the idea that his couples are secretly miserable. He points to his institute’s mandatory post-marital intervention program. If a couple he matched encounters friction—whether six months or six years after the wedding—they are required by their initial agreement to return to his office for mediation before taking any legal steps toward separation.

"I do not just perform the ceremony and walk away," Ardabili says. "I am a stakeholder in their home. When they fight, they come to me. I act as an arbiter, a counselor, and a spiritual guide."

---

### A Microcosm of a Society at a Crossroads

In many ways, Jafar Ardabili’s institute is a microcosm of modern Iran’s central paradox: an ancient civilization attempting to solve hyper-modern crisis using adapted traditional tools.

On a rainy Tuesday afternoon in Tehran, the waiting room outside Ardabili’s office is full. A young engineer sits anxiously, adjusting his collar, while across from him, a mother in a black *chador* quietly flips through a binder of profiles on behalf of her daughter, a medical student.

They are here because the modern world—with its dating apps, economic uncertainty, and shifting social contracts—has left them disoriented. In Ardabili, they see a bridge between the security of the past and the realities of the present.

Whether his zero-divorce record is a literal statistical truth or a byproduct of rigorous selection and cultural conditioning, one thing remains clear: in a society undergoing a turbulent social revolution, the cleric of Tehran has tapped into a profound human desire—the yearning for a promise that actually lasts.
